subject: Computer Networking
title: Aloha and Early Wireless
description: One-minute skill: Aloha and Early Wireless.

hook.text: In 1970s Hawaii, researchers wanted to connect island campuses without cables. They used radio waves.

buildup.text: ALOHAnet was one of the first wireless data networks. Stations transmitted whenever they had data to send.

discovery.text: If two stations transmitted at once, their signals collided. A simple retry mechanism handled the conflict.

twist.text: This collision-and-retry concept became the basis of Ethernet. Bob Metcalfe adapted it for wired networks.

climax.text: From a small island experiment, the ideas behind ALOHAnet shaped how billions of devices share networks today.

punchline.text: Wi-Fi and Ethernet both trace back to a Hawaiian experiment.

quiz.question: What networking concept originated from ALOHAnet?

details.summary: ALOHAnet, created at the University of Hawaii in 1971, was the first wireless packet data network. It connected computers across the Hawaiian islands using UHF radio. Its random access protocol for sharing a wireless channel directly inspired Ethernet and all modern wireless networking.
details.whyItMatters: ALOHAnet proved that computers could communicate wirelessly using packet switching. Its access protocol became the foundation for Ethernet and Wi-Fi.
takeaways: ALOHAnet was the first wireless packet data network in 1971
It used UHF radio to connect computers across Hawaiian islands
Its random access protocol inspired Ethernet's CSMA/CD

faq.question: How did ALOHAnet inspire Ethernet?
faq.answer: ALOHAnet let stations transmit whenever they had data. If transmissions collided, stations waited a random time and retried. Robert Metcalfe adapted this idea for wired networks, adding carrier sensing to check if the wire was busy before transmitting, creating CSMA/CD.

faq.question: Why was wireless networking important for Hawaii?
faq.answer: Hawaiian islands could not be connected with cables easily. Radio was the practical solution for linking university campuses across the island chain. The geographical challenge drove innovation in wireless packet networking that proved useful far beyond Hawaii.
